newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Minister seeks troops if Chechnya Russians harmed.
newsitem.headline: Minister seeks troops if Chechnya Russians harmed.

text.p: Russia should intervene militarily in Chechnya if Russians still living in the breakaway region come under attack, the interior minister said on Friday, 10 days before scheduled presidential elections there.
"If it comes to a real genocide in Chechnya it is Russia that should protect Russians there and save them from arbitrary rule even by sending troops," Anatoly Kulikov told a press conference.

The fate of Russians remaining in Chechnya is causing growing concern in Moscow, although some observers say politicians are highlighting the issue to give them an excuse to say the vote is invalid if Chechens elect a hardline president.

"There's complete chaos in Chechnya," Dmitry Rogozin, who heads the Congress of Russian Communities political movement, said on Friday. "Almost all the guarantees the Chechens have made on protecting Russians have been broken."

Before Yeltsin launched a full-scale military assault to crush Chechnya's separatists in December 1994 about 400,000 ethnic Russians lived there, about a third of the total population. Many of the few that remain are elderly and very poor, living amid rubble.
Cossacks, descendants of men who led imperial Russia's drive into the Caucasus in the 19th century, are also seeking the right to bear arms in defence of the remaining Russians in Chechnya.
They have asked the Russian government for the right to intervene in two areas of Chechnya they say historically belong to them as well as guard Russia's internal border with Chechnya.

"We would like to restore the traditional Cossack regiments," the leader of a regional Cossack group wrote in a recent open letter to Yeltsin. "And we can find experienced officers and generals to oppose the (Chechen) field commanders."
Kulikov rejected the demand on Friday. "I strongly oppose the idea of arming Cossacks," he said. "If we try to arm Cossacks living in Chechnya this will speed up their extermination."
If Chechens threaten the safety of the Russians in Chechnya, Moscow itself should intervene, said Kulikov, who led part of the 21-month military operation against Grozny.

But the deputy secretary of the Russian Security Council, Boris Berezovsky, told Cossacks on Wednesday that if the government did not support their proposal to arm them, he would step down, NTV television reported.
Tens of thousands of Cossacks, known for their dapper military uniforms, curly moustaches and tall wool hats, live in Russia, most based in the southern Don valley.

Some observers say Moscow might play on concerns about ethnic Russians in Chechnya if the January 27 presidential vote brings to power a militant leader such as Shamil Basayev, a guerrilla commander who led a hostage-taking raid into Russia last year in which more than 100 people died.

"If the citizens elect irreconcilable separatist Basayev, then Russia's last hope to save face would be to not recognise the legitimacy of the elections," the mass-circulation Moskovsky Komsomolets newspaper wrote on Friday.

Among the recent incidents causing concern were the murder of several Russian families in the Chechen capital Grozny in late December, and an attack on a train in Chechnya on Tuesday en route to Moscow. During that attack, one policeman was killed and several others wounded, Itar-Tass news agency reported.
Rogozin, whose movement has been allied with Yeltsin's ex-security chief and current foe Alexander Lebed, said Chechens also planned to attack pilots in Russia who bombarded Grozny during the war.
